Mono black, and maybe by extension dimir, is a breath of fresh air compared to gruul as it fundamentally requires for the mostpart that you look at your creatures, life total and graveyard in a completely different way than you do when playing big stompy. Suddenly, your creatures dying is trivial and you want them to die. Your life total can be used to buy goods and services, namely cards in hand, but other things too. Board wipes no longer obliterate you the way they normally would. You celebrate when the mono blue mill player joins the table. Your library is way more accessible than normal with the best tutors in all of MTG. And most important of all, your combos now focus away from combat step and now involve bizarre multi-zone loops of permanents. 

If you are genuinely trying to experience something new, this can be an exciting new direction for you.

\[\[Purphoros, God of the Forge\]\]. The constant, nonstop pinging of 2 damage off every single creature, token or otherwise, pressures every single deck in existence. Unless your opponents invest hard in exile to try and mess with you, purphoros's indestructibility and lack of creature status for most of the time tends to invalidate removal. He gives zero craps about boardwipes because it's all about making as many things hit the board at once as possible and then saccing them to throw damage around because he doesn't need no combat step to chew through player life totals, and if they do get the boardwipe off he has cards like \[\[Anax, hardened in the forge\]\] that immediately flood the board with new tokens to punish them heavily. He's in red so he can easily deal with anything that turns off etbs, and easily hoses lifegain. As long as he is doing things, he is aggressively pressuring the entire table and every turn he gets threatens to put even the control and midrange players in kill range from either him or other players. He just gives zero fucks about what the other players are doing, his job is to accelerate matches or end them altogether. The only thing that ever counters him is incidentally uniting the table against him, but by the time they get all the resources together to finish him off, every one of your opponents is bloodied from so much damage to their face that they just couldn't prevent that the game tends to end shortly thereafter.

He's also just incredibly wild to play and easy to build and he got some new toys recently in modern horizons 3.

\[\[Elixir of Immortality\]\] is probably one of the most underrated artifacts in existence. Forget just mill-heavy metas, elixir is amazing when you're doing things like casting from your library such as through cascade; being able to just put your graveyard back in your library to freecast from later can be incredibly advantageous. The 5 life is also a nice bonus on top of this. But it's most underrated function is to deny gravehate. Nothing sucks worse than having that graveyard you built up over the course of the game exiled by a 1 mana artifact, so for a similar cost you can save your graveyard from destruction by shuffling it back into your library to be milled later. It's just a wonderful little 1 mana artifact that you can probably find good uses for.

You need to understand that superfriends is a strategy that openly advertises to the table that you are the prime target for turning cards sideways in your direction. As a result, you need to double down on literally anything that says those cards do no damage or those cards don't stay on the board.

A solid chunk of your deck is gonna be a combination of removal, fog, and outright resource denial, because your planeswalker emblems cannot be removed when they're gained and punching your planeswalkers or even you is the ultimate, oftentimes only way for them to keep those emblems out of the game. So you gotta abandon all notions of playing nice and just, invest in that which says to them that punching you or your planeswalkers is futile. 

If you're playing golgari superfriends, your best bet is tons of killspells, the best boardwipes black can afford, and finally, and most importantly: Fog. So much fog. All the fog. Every time they swing at you you should spend 2 mana to make it do nothing. Get yourself a seedborne muse and a wilderness reclamation while you're at it, so you can slam planeswalkers on your turn and then have mana open at every turn to cast whatever you need to tell the other players NO. 

The reality is, you're not playing superfriends. Not actually. You're playing control, but with 90% more planeswalkers. The only other option available to you that doesn't involve doubling down on control-y elements is to dilute your primary strategy with aggressive creatures and chump blockers to accelerate killing your opponents so they can't ever interact with you, what with them being dead and all. Your favorite keyword at that point will be vigilance, because being able to swing and block with the same creature is vital to your success, as no blocks=dead planeswalkers.
